To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the incidence of hepatocellar carcinoma is expected to increase in the next two decades in the United States, 2) the incidence of HCC can be reduced in patients with hepatitis C cirrhoses by curing the hepatitis, 3) several noncurative treatments reduce the incidence of hepatellular carcinoma in patients who have chronic hepatitis C, and 4) numerous agents prevent or reduce the development of HCC in animal models.

(i) chronic hepatitis C is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma and (ii) several agents reduce the risk of developing this cancer in chronic hepatitis C. Chemoprevention is defined as the use of natural, biological or synthetic chemicals to reduce the risk for, or delay the onset or development of, premalignant or malignant diseases (1).
chemopreventative agents can reduce hepatocellular carcinoma risk in patients with chronic HCV infection, and that these agents include carotenoids, coffee, SAMe, vitamin K₂, and polyprenoic acids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of chemoprevention agents for hepatocellular carcinoma, the most common form of primary liver cancer, in patients with chronic liver disease due to hepatitis C virus (HVC) infection.
the development of new therapeutic agents for the treatment of chronic liver diseases and hepatocarcinoma.

the development of new chemotherapeutic agents for hepatocellular carcinoma, and with the evaluation of the potential chemoprevention properties of several natural and synthetic compounds in animal models of liver cancer, and in patients with chronic liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the available data are insufficient to recommend any chemopreventative agent for patients with chronic hepatitis and HCV infection.
the data are insufficient at present to support the use of chemoprevention in patients with hepatitis C.
the data are not conclusive, but that there is a strong rationale and some evidence to support chemoprevention trials of agents with known hepatocarcinogenetic effects in chronic hepatitis C.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chemopreventative agents can be used in the management of HCC.
the use of SAMe as a chemoprevention in patients with chronic HCV is an achievable objective.
the use of SAMe in the treatment of chronic hepatitis C is safe and well tolerated, and may have a beneficial impact on the progression of liver disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for large-scale, well-controlled, prospective trials of chemopreventative agents in hepatitis C cirrhotics.
chemopreventative agents may reduce hepatocellular carcinoma risk in patients with chronic HCV infection, and may be particularly useful in those who are not cured of their HCV infection.
there are several agents that have shown promise in preventing hepatocellular carcinoma, and these should be evaluated in randomized controlled clinical trials.
